articles.title: Feijóo convirtió el debate con Sánchez en una ofensiva preparada durante semanas: un dossier con 400 páginas y una siesta la misma tarde
articles.standfirst: El candidato popular llegó con la estrategia de cuestionar la gestión del Gobierno y poner al presidente contra las cuerdas
articles.summary: El candidato popular llegó con la estrategia de cuestionar la gestión del Gobierno y poner al presidente contra las cuerdas
articles.body: Alberto Núñez Feijóo fue al debate electoral con una estrategia trabajada semanas atrás. El líder del Partido Popular había ensayado tanto su intervención que sabía que podría usarse como una forma de consolidar su posición entre los votantes indecisos: su equipo había preparado un dossier de 400 páginas con críticas a la gestión del Ejecutivo (un documento que el candidato estudió y memorizó mientras viajaba por España durante la campaña). La preparación se tradujo rápidamente en su intervención. Feijóo utilizó datos económicos para cuestionar la situación del país y centrarse en el aumento del costo de vida: “La leche ha subido un 53%, los huevos un 91%, las patatas un 60%, las legumbres un 110%”, dijo en el enfrentamiento. El candidato utilizó estos datos para reforzar los reproches contra el presidente del Gobierno. El líder popular también fue directamente contra Sánchez con preguntas específicas que podrían dañarlo: “Voy a hacerle algunas preguntas concretas porque eso es lo que la gente quiere saber. ¿Manipuló votos en las primarias de su partido? ¿Sí o no?”. Feijóo quería tomar la iniciativa y obligar al presidente a reaccionar. El comportamiento del candidato también fue parte de la preparación. Su entorno dijo que Feijóo llegó tranquilo el día del debate, tomando incluso una siesta y chateando por WhatsApp con sus colaboradores. Esa actitud se mostró luego frente a las cámaras donde proyectó seguridad y confianza, a tenor de las reacciones en redes sociales. Durante el cara a cara, el popular insistió en continuar sus intervenciones incluso cuando las interrupciones dificultaban el intercambio de argumentos. “¿Puedo continuar mi reflexión?”, preguntó en uno de esos momentos antes de reclamar su turno para hablar. La estrategia no sólo era imponerse dialécticamente sobre Sánchez. El candidato gallego se basó en la iniciativa, firmeza y convencer a aquellos que aún no habían decidido si votarían por él o no. El debate le dio protagonismo y reforzó una imagen de estar listo para disputar la presidencia del Gobierno, según los expertos.

articles.title: Impeaching Hegseth is a trap Democrats should avoid
articles.summary: Many Republicans acknowledge privately that Pete Hegseth is unfit to serve as secretary of Defense. That doesn’t mean House Democrats should impeach him when they take control in January. Impeachment is a political remedy for serious misconduct in office that is rarely used and seldom results in a conviction by the Senate, especially when it…
articles.body:
Many Republicans acknowledge privately that Pete Hegseth is unfit to serve as secretary of Defense. That doesn’t mean House Democrats should impeach him when they take control in January.

Impeachment is a political remedy for serious misconduct in office that is rarely used and seldom results in a conviction by the Senate, especially when it is widely viewed as a partisan act.

Only two Cabinet secretaries have ever been impeached . William Belknap, President Grant’s secretary of War, resigned shortly before the House voted unanimously in 1876 to impeach him. In 2024, Republicans impeached Alejandro Mayorkas, President Biden’s secretary of Homeland Security, only to have the Senate dismiss the charges without a trial.

Three presidents have been impeached, all largely along partisan lines . Andrew Johnson, Bill Clinton and President Trump were all acquitted in the Senate. Impeachment weakened Johnson , but Clinton emerged politically strengthened , at least temporarily, and Trump’s impeachments did little to diminish his support among Republicans.

Impeachment is unlikely to remove Hegseth or change administration policy. If every senator votes, Democrats would have to convince at least 11 Republicans to secure the two-thirds majority needed to convict — a highly unlikely outcome.

Two weeks ago, outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R.-Ky.) moved to impeach Hegseth for actions ranging from waging war against Iran without congressional authorization to retaliating against Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) for criticizing military policy. Every Democrat who voted joined Massie, the lone Republican, in opposing a motion to refer the resolution to the Judiciary Committee. The motion nonetheless passed 211-204, effectively shelving impeachment for the remainder of this Congress.

Several leading progressives quickly declared that Democrats should press ahead with impeachment when they take control of Congress in January. “We need to raise it up back again as soon as possible,” Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D.-N.Y.) insisted . “We should do it as soon as we can,” added Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) Asked whether Democrats should hold hearings first, Khanna replied, “No, we should just push it.”

Whether Hegseth’s actions constitute high crimes and misdemeanors is debatable. But the more important question for Democrats is political: How can they hold the administration accountable without undermining the affordability agenda voters expect them to pursue?

Most voters will likely see impeachment as an effort to attack Trump by proxy. The initiative will also allow Hegseth to claim vindication if the Senate fails to convict, as Trump and the Pentagon did when Massie’s impeachment resolution was sent to committee.

Democratic leaders have already voiced opposition to “snap” impeachments . Although they supported Massie’s resolution, they did not introduce it themselves. Once they control the House, they will own a decision to proceed. They should insist on investigations and hearings before reaching conclusions.

The main charges in Massie’s eight articles of impeachment concern decisions made by Trump, including the war against Iran, military operations in Yemen, the kidnapping of Venezuela’s president, and military strikes on suspected drug boats in the Caribbean.

Following orders does not absolve Hegseth if he knew or should have known the orders were unlawful. But executive branch legal opinions defending some of these operations, however dubious , give Hegseth (and Trump) considerable legal cover.

To be sure, some of Massie’s articles focus on conduct for which Hegseth bears primary responsibility. They include dismantling safeguards designed to minimize civilian casualties and censuring Kelly for reminding members of the military they have a duty not to obey illegal orders. Other charges could be added, such as mishandling classified information , obstructing congressional oversight , politicizing the officer corps and engaging in favoritism in contracting .

Oversight hearings with sworn testimony and documentary evidence could help the public understand how damaging Hegseth’s tenure has been. They might establish, for example, whether he ordered attacks against the survivors of one or more boat strikes — a crime by almost anyone’s definition — or whether, as he claims, Adm. Frank “Mitch” Bradley was responsible.

Hearings might also highlight Hegseth’s failure to keep Congress informed about spending, his decision to fire a large number of high-ranking officers , his mishandling of military operations, including the depletion of high-end weapons during the war in Iran, and whether he played a role in the bombing of a primary school on February 28 that killed more than 100 children.

In the process, Democrats might attract some bipartisan support for other avenues of accountability, whether through legislation, restrictions on appropriations, or censure.

The first serious test for incoming Democratic leaders may be whether they can resist demands for immediate impeachment from within their own caucus. All it takes is one House member to introduce an impeachment resolution. And many Democrats, including Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), likely the next Speaker of the House, have indicated they are “ hard yes ” supporters of impeachment.

Jeffries and other Democratic leaders, however, appear to understand both the politics of impeachment and the Senate math. Faced with an impeachment resolution, they would be wise to send it to a committee — not to derail accountability, but to establish a foundation for it.

Democrats were elected to govern, not settle scores. They need to show they can pursue accountability responsibly while also addressing the cost of living, health care and other issues on which their electoral success rests. They must not allow themselves to sprint into a dead-end street.

David Wippman is emeritus president of Hamilton College. Glenn C. Altschuler is the Thomas and Dorothy Litwin Emeritus Professor of American Studies at Cornell University.

articles.title: Cornyn calls Cruz ‘fragile thing’ amid Texas judgeship dispute
articles.summary: Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) on Saturday called Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) a “fragile thing” amid the former’s dispute over a judicial nominee for Texas not being a Texan. “Everyone knows that I am a notorious cusser and screamer and that Ted is a fragile thing,” Cornyn wrote on social media Saturday. “But enough about us.…
articles.body:
Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) on Saturday called Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) a “fragile thing” amid the former’s dispute over a judicial nominee for Texas not being a Texan .

“Everyone knows that I am a notorious cusser and screamer and that Ted is a fragile thing,” Cornyn wrote on social media Saturday. “But enough about us. If a President can appoint someone from another state, no Senator will have a say in their state, notwithstanding Article II, Section 2, Clause 2 of the U.S. Constitution. It is called ‘advise and consent.’”

Cornyn was responding to Cruz’s Saturday interview with Fox News. Cruz spoke with anchor Kayleigh McEnany about a reported shouting match on the Senate floor Friday regarding T. Elliot Gaiser, President Trump’s judicial nominee for the U.S. District Court in the Northern District of Texas, according to The Washington Sun .

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

Cornyn blocked Gaiser’s nomination Wednesday by not filing a blue slip, where the Senate Judiciary Committee chair asks home-state senators to assess a nominee. If withheld or returned with rejections, the process does not generally proceed.

Cornyn had told outlets after blocking Gaiser last week that the nominee was not a Texan and had no trial experience. Gaiser lived in Ohio before he was tapped to lead the Office of Legal Counsel at the Department of Justice.

Cruz made the case for Gaiser, saying that the nominee’s wife is from Texas and her family lives in Dallas and wanted to return to the Lone Star State “to live near her family.”

McEnany asked about the verbal confrontation, saying The Washington Sun reported that Cornyn told Cruz that he was “‘upset at someone ending my career,’” and it wasn’t clear if Cornyn was referring to Cruz or to President Trump.

She said Fox News reached out to Cornyn’s office and was told, “We will let you know if I have anything for you on that,” before asking Cruz if the incident happened.

The junior Texas senator said Cornyn was upset and asked if he would meet with Gaiser, which Cornyn refused. When Cruz said he told his colleague that this would cede the vacancy to the Democrats when they take control of the Senate in January, “unfortunately, he got very angry.”

“He began screaming, he began cursing at me, and the reason it got reported is there were reporters sitting there watching,” Cruz continued. “And he was yelling loud enough that what’s been reported are the things that he was screaming and cursing at the top of his lungs.”

The Sun reported that during the exchange on the Senate floor, Cornyn yelled at Cruz, “I don’t find you credible. I’m mad at you!”

Reporters were unable to hear Cruz’s reply, but Cornyn yelled back, “Oh, that’s bulls—!” He waved off Cruz with his hand and walked away.

“Listen Kayleigh, it is tough in politics when you lose an election,” Cruz said, referring to Cornyn’s loss in the Republican Senate primary, which ultimately led to Democratic Sen.-elect James Talarico winning Cornyn’s seat .

“That is always hard on anybody, and we’ve got a lot of people who’ve lost their elections who are angry and sometimes, when they’re angry, they lash out,” he noted.

Cruz concluded that he wished “it wasn’t the people of Texas that were paying the price.”

articles.title: $1.7 trillion Biden-era government funding bill found unconstitutional, appeals court rules
articles.summary: An appeals court ruled Friday that the 2022 $1.7 trillion government funding bill passed by Congress under former President Biden through a pandemic-era rule that allowed lawmakers to vote by proxy was unconstitutional. The New Orleans-based 5th U.S. Circuit ‌Court of Appeals voted 9-8, stating that voting by proxy went against the Constitution’s Quorum Clause…
articles.body:
An appeals court ruled Friday that the 2022 $1.7 trillion government funding bill passed by Congress under former President Biden through a pandemic-era rule that allowed lawmakers to vote by proxy was unconstitutional.

The New Orleans-based 5th U.S. Circuit ‌Court of Appeals voted 9-8, stating that voting by proxy went against the Constitution’s Quorum Clause as its “text, context, original understanding and unbroken historical application all indicate that Members of Congress must be present for quorum purposes.”

“‘Proxy presence’ does not count,” U.S. Circuit Judge Cory Wilson, a Trump appointee, wrote in the ruling. “While the chambers of the legislature have much discretion regarding their rules of procedure, the Quorum Clause’s constraints on congressional power cannot be circumvented by congressional fiat.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The House used the proxy rule when the 2023 Consolidated Appropriations Act was passed 225-201, with 226 House members recording their presence and their vote by proxy.

“Thus, when the House voted on the Act, less than a majority of members were physically present,” Wilson wrote.

He noted how the rule was implemented during the COVID-19 pandemic, in which voting by proxy preventing the risk of the virus spreading when infections were still high. He also established that the federal government’s “theory” was that Congress could define what “present” means for the purposes of holding quorum.

He added, however, that the fact that it was implemented in response to the pandemic “does nothing to minimize the ramifications of the Government’s theory, because nothing about that theory depends on the existence of an emergency.”

“Under the Government’s view, the House needs no external justification whatsoever before allowing Members to delegate their presence to a proxy for quorum purposes,” Wilson wrote. “While an ’emergency may afford a reason for the exertion of a living power already enjoyed,’ an emergency ‘may not call into life a power which has never lived.'”

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R), who earlier this month lost his Senate bid, brought the case in 2023 to block the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act from being enforced in Texas.

Wilson wrote that the decision does not extend further to the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act’s impact on Texas beyond “affirming the relief awarded by the district court.”

Judge James Graves Jr., an Obama appointee, wrote in the dissenting opinion that the majority had misinterpreted the Constitution and that no member of the House objected that there was a lack of quorum. He added that requiring lawmakers to be in person “shoehorns a much larger requirement into the Constitution.”

He also noted that 99 percent of lawmakers took part in the vote on the omnibus bill.

“Put simply, historical practice over the last 235 years strongly favors rejecting the majority’s narrow interpretation,” Graves wrote. “Even the First Congress, which included Framers of our national charter, well understood that physical attendance was not required by the Quorum Clause.”

articles.title: Congress can protect children with craniofacial anomalies
articles.summary: Advocates for the Enabling Lasting Smiles Act continue to urge Congress to pass the bipartisan legislation to ensure insurance coverage for medically necessary care for children born with craniofacial anomalies.
articles.body:
I vividly remember sitting in the dental clinic at Children’s Wisconsin, listening as the care team explained my five-year-old son’s diagnosis and future. Hearing that a child so young would need dentures and braces and ultimately further down the road bone-grafting, and implants, was overwhelming. But the pediatric dental team was exceptional, offering both answers and hope: since his rare craniofacial condition required medically necessary care, insurance would cover his treatment plan. At the time, I had no idea that “craniofacial anomaly” would soon become a defining part of our family’s everyday language.

Throughout every complex care journey lies a relentless onslaught of critical decisions and constant anxiety. Families are left wrestling with difficult questions: Is this the right care team? Is this the most appropriate treatment plan? How much work can I afford to miss and what about the continual follow-up appointments? How do we manage hours on the road just to reach a specialist who knows how to treat this rare condition? Then comes the breaking point: an insurance denial that instantly turns into an unwarranted, full-time job just to get the coverage that’s medically necessary.

The moment the first denial arrived and labeled a five-year-old’s dentures as “cosmetic”, the harsh reality set in and we knew we would need to advocate for coverage. What followed were endless, exhausting hours over the phone, passing the phone to my husband whenever frustration would become too apparent. We found ourselves repeatedly explaining what a congenital anomaly is and why having teeth is medically necessary. The insult to injury? Being told that if an accident had taken his teeth, insurance would provide coverage for replacement, but because my son was simply born without them, through no fault of his own, he would not receive coverage.

There are very few things in life that strip away your dignity faster than begging an insurance representative to let your child chew, eat and speak. Over and over, I was brought to tears recounting the frequency of my son choking on his food and the isolation he felt at school when classmates couldn’t understand his speech. Having to justify why basic human functions are “medically necessary” is degrading and feels desperate. You pour your heart out to a stranger while listening to your child being reduced to a claim, a nameless file not deemed worthy of teeth or a smile. This changed me and it would change you too.

Before long, this absurd performance becomes your weekly, even daily, routine. The system feels intentionally designed to break you, draining every ounce of energy until you’re too exhausted to fight. That exhaustion carries over into every corner of your life, leaving you with a reoccurring question: How are children repeatedly denied the basic care they need just to eat, speak, hear and see?

What insurance companies failed to take into account is the perseverance and resilience of the craniofacial community. Over a decade ago, when my son was just 11 years old, he shared his story with Sen. Tammy Baldwin (D-Wis.), and inspired legislation that he named the Ensuring Lasting Smiles Act .

The bill would close loopholes and ensure that health plans cover outpatient and inpatient items and services related to the diagnosis and treatment of a congenital anomaly or birth defect that primarily impacts the appearance or function of the eyes, ears, teeth, mouth, or jaw. This commonsense bill is led by Sens. Baldwin and Joni Ernst (R-Iowa) and Reps. Neal Dunn (R-Fla.) and Kim Schrier (D-Wash.).

That single moment led to a nationwide advocacy initiative. For over a decade, families, children, and providers from across America have advocated side-by-side throughout the halls of Congress, bravely telling their stories and stories on behalf of their patients. They’ve watched the legislative clock run out each Congress, only to become more determined and start stronger during the next session.

These families raise funds to pay for medically necessary care for themselves and their children, then turn around and scrape together whatever it takes to travel to Washington, D.C. year after year. The bill’s advocates refuse to sit quietly while reckless delays and denials jeopardize their futures and their children’s futures. Through grassroots advocacy and relentless bravery, they have mindfully advocated to make sure their voices are heard.

The Ensuring Lasting Smiles Act is an anomaly of its own: a bicameral bill consistently garnering strong bipartisan support. It proves that despite political divides, both sides of the aisle can unite around a fundamental truth: every child deserves to eat, speak, breathe, see, and hear. Essential human functions that are basic human rights. It stands as a powerful example of what is possible when patients and providers advocate together, turning shared mission into lasting change for an entire community.

The momentum behind this bill is historic. In the 117th Congress, it moved forward through Congress with 62 Senate and 317 House co-sponsors, passing the House with a supermajority vote. Today, in the 119th Congress, support for the Ensuring Lasting Smiles Act is once again building, with 54 Senate and 227 House co-sponsors. A decade after this all began, my son is now 21 years old and an entire community of young advocates has grown up advocating in Washington.

The clock is ticking down once again for this session. Congress can immediately end these senseless barriers for children born with craniofacial anomalies. Our children deserve a lifetime of smiles. It’s time for Congress to protect them and pass the Ensuring Lasting Smiles Act.

Becky M. Abbott, MPH, is from Slinger, Wis., and an ELSA Coalition advocate.

articles.title: Trump says it will be ‘very hard’ to work with Schumer as Senate majority leader
articles.summary: President Trump said Sunday that it would be “very hard” for him to work with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) if he becomes majority leader next year, as the New York Democrat faces a challenge to his leadership post when Democrats take control of the chamber in January. “It is going to be very…
articles.body:
President Trump said Sunday that it would be “very hard” for him to work with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) if he becomes majority leader next year, as the New York Democrat faces a challenge to his leadership post when Democrats take control of the chamber in January.

“It is going to be very hard for me to work with Chuck Schumer should he become Senate Majority Leader,” Trump wrote Sunday on Truth Social .

“He failed badly as ‘Leader’ once before, one of the worst history, and I have little doubt that he will fail again,” he continued. “All he did was perpetuate the Russia, Russia, Russia Hoax, and many other Hoaxes and Scams, making my victory in 2024 an easy and glorious one.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

Trump faces the prospect of working with a Democratic-controlled Congress for the final two years of his presidency. Democrats’ victories in both chambers during the midterms means the president will need their cooperation to advance legislation and secure Senate confirmations for future nominees.

Schumer faces a challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who is seeking to unseat the longtime Democratic leader following the party’s sweeping victories in the midterm elections. Van Hollen said Friday that the race remains “ wide-open ,” despite Schumer’s insistence that he has enough votes to retain his position.

“I’m the underdog in this race. After all, the incumbent has the powers of incumbency, but the reality is this is a wide-open race,” Van Hollen said on “The MeidasTouch Podcast.”

Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats since 2017, has publicly secured the support of 15 senators, compared with five for Van Hollen, according to The Hill’s whip list . Another 34 senators have not publicly declared their support for either candidate. The winner needs 28.

The Maryland Democrat has picked up endorsements from Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) and progressive Sens.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) and Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.), who have called for a new generation of Democratic leadership.

Schumer, however, has maintained that he has the votes to win the Dec. 1 leadership election.

“I’m confident I’ll be the next leader,” Schumer told reporters Tuesday. “I have the votes and we’re all going to roll up our sleeves and we’re going to focus on lowering costs, ending corruption.”

articles.title: Clayton says he trusts Trump ‘completely’ after calling Putin a friend
articles.summary: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton on Sunday said he trusts President Trump “completely” after Trump called Russian President Vladimir Putin, a perceived U.S. adversary, a friend. During Clayton’s interview with CNN’s “State of the Union” on Sunday, host Dana Bash showed the director of national intelligence two Truth Social posts from Trump referring to…
articles.body:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton on Sunday said he trusts President Trump “completely” after Trump called Russian President Vladimir Putin, a perceived U.S. adversary, a friend.

During Clayton’s interview with CNN’s “State of the Union” on Sunday, host Dana Bash showed the director of national intelligence two Truth Social posts from Trump referring to Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping as his friends , prompting her to ask Clayton if he thinks Putin is a friend to the U.S.

“The president is the greatest conductor of foreign policy, in a very challenging time … getting the three nuclear powers together and getting them to agree that they are not going to escalate, that they are going to communicate. That is historic. That is remarkable,” Clayton said.

“And in that context, whatever language the president wants to use, I trust him completely,” he added.

Bash pressed Clayton further on the question, asking if he thought Putin was a friend to the U.S.

“Dana, in different contexts, you can use a different word,” he replied. “The president pulling off that summit, getting the three of them together, is just remarkable.”

Trump, who has long had a friendly relationship with Putin, met with the Russian leader and Xi at a planned trilateral in Shenzhen, China. After arriving for a meeting Thursday, Trump said before approaching Putin, “ Who is he? He’s my friend .”

The meeting was meant to focus on paths toward peace in the Russia-Ukraine war and the Iran war, as well as push for denuclearization. The three superpowers established a “ declaration toward peace ,” which addressed United Nations reform; oil production and supply; the International Criminal Court; and nuclear conflict, according to text released by all three countries.

Trump early last week told reporters he believed the Russian president was “backing down a bit” in the war in Ukraine, which will hit the five-year mark in February.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who has fought off Russian military advances with help from the U.S. and Europe, told reporters Saturday that the summit “turned out very badly for Russia.”

“Putin didn’t get his ‘Yalta 2,’” Zelensky wrote Saturday on the social platform X , referring to 1945 talks held by the Allied powers on how to finally defeat Nazi Germany. “… Did Putin want a real Yalta? Yes. In the sense of carving up the world and changing borders. China didn’t let itself be drawn into it. I don’t know what happened between the United States and Russia in their bilateral, but Ukraine wasn’t discussed.”

Zelensky continued the Yalta analogy with: “If there really was an intention to reaffirm the victory over fascism now, then the participants at this summit would have to be the United States, Europe, and Ukraine. Definitely not Russia … If Putin wanted to remind the world once again who he is, there was no need –– we haven’t forgotten that he’s a terrorist and a killer.”

articles.title: The cost of loyalty: Kamala Harris’s legacy on Gaza will haunt her in 2028
articles.summary: The former VP cannot realistically hope to wipe the political slate clean.
articles.body:
Kamala Harris has just reminded Democrats of one big reason why nominating her for president in 2028 would be a mistake.

Last month, before the historic midterm elections , the former vice president criticized “the failure to use our leverage to curtail the Israeli government’s horrific conduct in the war in Gaza.” She spoke not only of “the current administration” but also “our administration before, where we should have acted sooner and more forcefully.”

It was a truthful statement, but it came two years too late.

In October 2024, as the Democratic nominee for president, Harris was asked on the ABC program “The View,” “Would you have done something differently than President Biden during the past four years?”

“There is not a thing that comes to mind,” Harris replied .

That response was consistent with her unwavering support for President Biden’s huge shipments of weapons to Israel, which were then used to kill tens of thousands of Palestinian civilians in Gaza. Harris backed those shipments , which enabled the Israeli conduct that she now calls “horrific.”

Looking ahead, what could Harris possibly say or do to make up for that record? There is not a thing that comes to mind.

Harris did not just bypass moral considerations. She also engaged in political malpractice by placing her loyalty to Biden above electoral considerations as presidential nominee, thus weakening her chances of preventing Donald Trump’s return to the White House.

This is not mere hindsight. By early June 2024 — more than a month before Biden withdrew from the race — polling showed that most of the electorate wanted a halt to arming Israel. A CBS News-YouGov poll found that Americans opposed sending “weapons and supplies to Israel” 61-39 percent.

Yet Harris continued to repeat the Biden administration’s talking points while remaining tone-deaf to the domestic politics of the Gaza war. In August, the same month she was formally nominated at the Democratic convention, a YouGov poll in the swing states of Arizona, Georgia and Pennsylvania found that by a ratio of at least five-to-one, Democratic and independent voters said they’d be more likely to cast their ballots for Harris if she would support a cutoff of arms to Israel compared to those who said the opposite.

Now, two years after her loss to Trump, with survey results overwhelmingly negative toward arming Israel, Harris is playing catch-up. Perhaps it’s all well and good for her to acknowledge “failure to use our leverage” against Israel’s “horrific conduct” in Gaza. But shifting with the political winds is not the kind of party leadership that Democrats need.

Harris cannot realistically hope to wipe the political slate clean. Her handling of the Gaza issue was far more than simply a political misstep, and it is a subject that continues to strongly resonate with countless Democrats at the grassroots. If she goes back on the campaign trail to seek the 2028 nomination, the smoldering distrust and anger of many primary voters will follow her.

Disruptions of Harris stump speeches from protesters, denouncing her as complicit with Israel’s actions in Gaza, would predictably dog a Harris ’28 campaign. Critiques from some primary rivals would remind Democratic voters that she never spoke up against those actions when doing so could have made a difference. For many, Harris would represent a tragic era best left behind.

Another Harris campaign would rip open political wounds that she inflicted on herself and the party in 2024 by dutifully echoing Biden as the Gaza war went on. And Harris lacked the courage to interfere with the carnage in the Middle East throughout the last 15 months of the Biden presidency.

Of course, the vast majority of Democrats would vote for Harris in 2028 if it came down to her versus Vice President JD Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio. But that would be a high jump over low standards. The Democratic Party and the nation deserve better.

Norman Solomon is co-founder of RootsAction and executive director of the Institute for Public Accuracy. His latest book is “ The Blue Road to Trump Hell: How Corporate Democrats Paved the Way for Autocracy . “

articles.title: Army plans to proceed with lead azide detonation despite indefinite pause
articles.summary: The U.S. Army is planning to proceed with its detonation of lead azide despite a federal court ordering an indefinite pause by invoking the emergency munitions and explosives exclusion, according to new court filings. “The Army must perform a controlled detonation to protect the public from the more significant threat from an uncontrolled explosion, and…
articles.body:
The U.S. Army is planning to proceed with its detonation of lead azide despite a federal court ordering an indefinite pause by invoking the emergency munitions and explosives exclusion, according to new court filings .

“The Army must perform a controlled detonation to protect the public from the more significant threat from an uncontrolled explosion, and the Army intends to act by November 24,” lawyers for the Department of Justice (DOJ) wrote.

The Army initially planned two detonations of more than 60 barrels of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, but a federal court halted the planned explosion Friday. At the time, environmental groups stressed that the activity could expose thousands of families in the surrounding communities to toxic dust.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

The detonations were rescheduled to Monday, though the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals granted another emergency motion to indefinitely pause the explosions.

In new court filings, the DOJ argued that it didn’t need to follow the blocks due to the public safety risks the barrels of lead azide pose if left undetonated.

“To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action,” the attorneys asserted. “Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay.”

The initial complaint , filed by the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter, stated that the detonations would release elevated levels of lead dust into the air that could extend 100 miles north of the ammunition plant, leaving it to linger in “yards, gardens, and play areas” for years to come.

Inhaling or swallowing lead is highly dangerous to animals and humans, particularly children, and can pose serious health risks, according to the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). There are no known safe levels of exposure.

On Friday, the Army stated it was coordinating with Health and Human Services (HHS) and the EPA to ensure “controlled detonation in Middletown, Iowa is conducted in the safest fashion possible.”

“Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized,” the agencies wrote in a joint statement .

articles.title: Raskin on potential 2028 run: ‘I’ll do whatever it takes’
articles.summary: Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) on Sunday addressed the possibility he might seek the Democratic nomination for president in 2028, saying he will “do whatever it takes” if the party pushed him toward that. Raskin initially said he was not ruling out a presidential run in a report from The Baltimore Sun last week, which CNN’s…
articles.body:
Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) on Sunday addressed the possibility he might seek the Democratic nomination for president in 2028, saying he will “do whatever it takes” if the party pushed him toward that.

Raskin initially said he was not ruling out a presidential run in a report from The Baltimore Sun last week, which CNN’s Dana Bash brought up with the House member on “State of the Union.”

“Look, I have said from the very beginning, I want to get us through this period of massive lawlessness and corruption and authoritarianism,” he told her. “And I’ll do whatever it takes to do that and if my party wanted me to do that, I would do that.”

He said if he had party support to run for Senate “in another state,” he would do that too.

“But right now, all I’m focused on and concentrated on is to become the chairman of the House Judiciary Committee,” he continued. “We’ve got extraordinary new members who are coming to join us, and we have this avalanche of corruption that we’re facing, and we’re going to get to the bottom of it.”

Raskin concluded by saying he wants to “reestablish the rule of law under the Constitution,” and that’s “where I’m focusing all my energy.”

The Sun reported remarks Raskin made at an event at Towson University in Towson, Md., on Tuesday, where he said that if he “felt like I was the best person to run and win and do it, I would definitely consider it.”

“But we’ve got some serious talent out there,” he added.

Raskin’s name would add to a growing roster of names speculated to run in 2028, though no one has announced an official bid for the Democratic nomination. Potential names include California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D), former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and former Vice President Kamala Harris, among others.

Newsom has indicated that he would not run in 2028 if Harris, who worked with Newsom while he was mayor of San Francisco and she was the city’s district attorney, launched her own presidential bid.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), who made two runs for the party nomination in 2016 and 2020 but lost to former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and former President Biden, respectively, said last week he has no plans to run for president again.

“I think probably not. I think taking office at 87 years of age and finishing my first term at 91 is not something that probably inspires a whole lot of people,” Sanders told host Steven Bartlett on “The Diary of a CEO” podcast, later saying, “No, I’m not running for president.”

articles.title: Republicans are lucky 2026 wasn’t 2028
articles.summary: Had this hit in 2028, Democrats would have captured the federal government’s legislating trifecta.
articles.body:
After the 2026 midterms, Democrats will find it harder to get past Trump than Republicans will.

This could be a big liability in 2028 for Democrats, and one of Republicans’ few bright spots from their midterm debacle.

For Republicans finding silver linings in the midterms’ storm clouds isn’t easy. They were blown out, up and down ballots across the country. According to Real Clear Politics , they lost the generic House vote by nearly 14 points — just two years after winning the 2024 presidential popular vote by 1.5 points .

Their lopsided 2026 split translates into Republicans having already lost 43 House seats , currently putting them at their lowest number since 1993 . In the Senate, they have lost nine seats and are now at their lowest number since 2010 . Some House races are still undecided .

In the states, Republicans lost six governorships ; for the first time in 16 years Republicans will hold a minority of the nation’s governorships. In Congress and the states, it could take years for Republicans to recoup their losses — the 2026 Senate seats they lost won’t be up for election again until 2032.

Despite the dark clouds, there are some rays of light. Rep. Byron Donalds’ (R-Fla.) win for Florida governor is one. A Black conservative taking over the government reins in one of America’s best-run states and strongest economies is an opportunity to showcase conservative leadership in action and make inroads with a community that has historically been the Democrats’ near monopoly. In 2024 , 86 percent of Black voters went for Kamala Harris.

But the most important silver lining for Republicans is that 2026 wasn’t 2028. While the losses Republicans suffered this November are severe, their consequences pale in comparison to what they would have been if this blue wave landed in 2028.

For the next two years, Washington will be in gridlock. Yes, Democrats will control Congress. They can launch investigations, but few remember the ones they instigated in the House during the last two years of Trump’s first term. They can pass legislation, but Trump can veto it, and Republicans have ample votes to block Democrats overriding his vetoes. Democrats can even impeach, but they cannot remove their targets without many Republican votes.

Further, Trump has aggressively used executive orders in his administration and will undoubtedly continue to do so; congressional Democrats can do little about these.

For Trump, such a massive defeat will certainly be part of his legacy. Yet Bill Clinton suffered a mammoth wipeout in 1994, losing nine Senate seats and 54 House seats, and it’s arguable how many outside the inner sphere of politics remember.

In contrast to the stalemate 2026’s blue wave has most likely wrought, had this hit in 2028, Democrats would have captured the federal government’s legislating trifecta.

Weariness with two-term presidents by their second midterm is a historic fact. Yet, heading into November’s midterms, Republicans’ ability to get past Trump looked questionable. After all, he had won his party’s presidential nomination three consecutive times, a major party feat unseen since Franklin D. Roosevelt in 1940 , and the presidency twice. And he still exerted enormous influence on his party’s congressional nominees — now much to Republicans’ regret.

It’s now safe to say that after November, Republicans will have far greater interest in getting past Trump. In fact, their interest will be greater than that of the Democrats.

Democrats have not run a positive campaign since 2012, when they were enthusiastically backing Obama for a second term. They have been running against someone — specifically, against Trump — ever since. Since 2024, they have been running as moderates. While Democrats anti-Trump approach won’t change, their moderate one will likely have to.

Running against Trump in 2028 was already Democrats’ predilection; 2026’s results only confirms for them. Don’t expect them to change, even without Trump on the ballot.

Today, such a backward vision is an easily overlooked liability for Democrats. In two years, it won’t be. Presidential elections are about looking forward — to what you will do over the next four years — not about looking back at the last 12.

Further, Democrats’ successes since 2024 have come from running as moderates. Doing so is comparatively easy when you don’t have any power or expectations to meet. It becomes difficult once you have both and must deliver to your supporters, many of whom are not moderates themselves.

When Democrats last had full power in 2021 and 2022, they were anything but moderate with it. Although Democrats will only have full control of Congress for the next two years, they promise to be quite aggressive in using it. The result of Democrats’ last aggressive use of power was their repudiation in 2024.

In a footrace, running forward while looking back is difficult and dangerous. You run into things. In an electoral race, the thing you run into is the past — and the more aggressively you do, the greater your danger of colliding with an electorate who is looking ahead.

J.T. Young is the author of the recent book, “Unprecedented Assault: How Big Government Unleashed America’s Socialist Left” from RealClear Publishing.

articles.title: Clayton: Americans should prepare for system upgrades, warns of ‘bumps in the road’
articles.summary: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton on Sunday said Americans should prepare for upgrades to the country’s aging infrastructure and various systems, warning that there will be “bumps in the road” amid the recent spate of outages affecting businesses and air travel. “The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in…
articles.body:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton on Sunday said Americans should prepare for upgrades to the country’s aging infrastructure and various systems, warning that there will be “bumps in the road” amid the recent spate of outages affecting businesses and air travel.

“The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems,” he told CNN’s Dana Bash. “They should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road.”

Clayton compared it to refurbishing a home in that there’s “going to be things that you do not expect.”

Bash continued this analogy by adding that “it’s such that you have to leave, and you have to be prepared for alternate solutions.” She referred to comments made by Vice President Vance last week in response to Americans stocking up on food and water in preparation for a potential “crisis,” which Vance said was not coming, before she asked Clayton if Americans should stock up.

“America’s the most amazing and resilient place, and we have been living with interruptions,” he said. “Let’s give ourselves some credit. Let’s go back to COVID, other things –– Americans fought their way through these terrible things in an incredible, resilient way.”

“Could we be in a COVID situation? That was pretty intense,” Bash exclaimed.

“Not at all, not at all,” Clayton said. “Let me be clear. But what I’m saying is the American people are resilient, and when you’re straightforward with the American people about what’s going on, and that’s what we’re doing here. That’s what companies are doing.”

The series of outages affecting companies like Microsoft, Apple and United Airlines, as well as disruptions affecting access to JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo accounts, raised concerns about the country’s safety and whether bad actors were involved rather than incidents likely connected to upgrades.

Further outages that affected internal communication networks at the National Security Agency (NSA), and an outage that prompted the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to issue a nationwide ground stop, raised questions about whether these incidents were caused by cyberattacks.

U.S. intelligence leaders, including Clayton, have said this was not the case .

President Trump initially said “ it’s fine ” after these incidents, later saying that Americans stocking up on food and water should “ relax, everything’s fine .”

“I’ll let you know if there’s a problem,” he said in an interview with Fox News last Wednesday while in Shenzhen, China, before trilateral talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

articles.title: Director of National Intelligence: Putin is ‘not America’s friend in Ukraine’
articles.summary: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton defended President Trump’s use of the word “friend” to describe his relationship with Russian President Vladimir Putin but drew a distinction between the two leaders’ personal relationship and that of the country’s. In an interview with ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday, Clayton told co-anchor Jonathan Karl that the word…
articles.body:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton defended President Trump’s use of the word “friend” to describe his relationship with Russian President Vladimir Putin but drew a distinction between the two leaders’ personal relationship and that of the country’s.

In an interview with ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday, Clayton told co-anchor Jonathan Karl that the word “friend” was “entirely appropriate” in the context of last week’s summit in China.

“That conversation, that picture — historic, historic picture — was in the context of the three nuclear powers, the three main nuclear powers, getting together and saying, ‘We cannot have a nuclear incident,’” Clayton said Sunday.

At a White House press briefing on Friday, Trump declined to answer whether he considered the Russian president to be a friend to the U.S., saying he “can’t speak to America.”

“Is Vladimir Putin America’s friend? Because Trump said he couldn’t answer that question,” Karl asked Clayton.

“He is not America’s friend in Ukraine,” Clayton said of the Russian president. “Not at all.”

Clayton offered a similar defense of Trump during a separate appearance Sunday on CNN’s “State of the Union,” telling anchor Dana Bash that he trusts the president “completely” when it comes to his approach to foreign policy.

“The president is the greatest conductor of foreign policy, in a very challenging time,” Clayton said, praising Trump for bringing Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping together and securing an agreement to avoid escalating nuclear tensions.

Trump met with Putin and Xi in Shenzhen, where the president greeted the Russian leader by calling him “my friend.”

“And in that context, whatever language the president wants to use, I trust him completely,” he added.

When Bash asked directly whether he considered Putin a friend of the U.S., Clayton declined to give a definitive answer.

“In different contexts, you can use a different word,” he said.

articles.title: Democrats are laying off many of the people who just made their victory possible
articles.summary: Following recent layoffs within its digital operations, critics argue the Democratic National Committee must maintain permanent infrastructure to sustain its momentum leading toward the 2028 election.
articles.body:
After the 2024 election, the Democratic National Committee’s digital operation was, in the words of one of the people who later rebuilt it, “stripped for parts.”

Paulina Mangubat, the committee’s deputy chief mobilization officer, wrote about it last week in the industry newsletter “Link in Bio.” Much of the creator program was lost, the team was dismantled, and the work started over from scratch. So she set out to build something that would outlast a single election cycle and helped Democrats win back the internet. Then, last week, as Mangubat herself voluntarily departed the DNC, several of her colleagues were laid off.

On Nov. 2, DNC Chair Ken Martin was publicly touting the most successful social media cycle in party history: 8.5 billion views on branded content, 6.8 million new followers and nearly 4.3 billion additional views from FactPost, the committee’s unbranded operation. The team built a network of more than 700 independent creators with a combined following exceeding 175 million , supplied with clips they could turn into their own content and distribute to Americans who might never follow an official Democratic Party account. As a member of that creator network, I’ve seen firsthand how effectively the team gets content into the hands of people who can amplify it.

Then Democrats won both chambers of Congress. Now the DNC has laid off many of the people who helped make that victory possible .

Anyone who has worked in Democratic politics knows that staffing up ahead of an election and scaling back immediately afterward is standard practice. Indeed, the DNC filed a layoff notice on Sept. 14 , well before Democrats knew the magnitude of their coming midterm victory. Many of these positions were likely designed to be temporary from the outset. My objection is not that the DNC is departing from a standard off-cycle practice, but that it is adhering to a practice that no longer makes real strategic sense. Digital communications is one area of modern politics where the work between elections is every bit as important as the work during them.

Martin faces real financial constraints. The committee carries millions in debt and a significant cash disadvantage relative to the Republican National Committee . But Martin has already demonstrated that he understands the case for permanent infrastructure: His commitment of more than $1 million a month to state parties was premised on exactly that argument. It was a smart investment. But the logic should not stop at the state funding level.

I served on Hillary Clinton’s digital team in 2016 and have spent a decade watching our party treat online communication as a seasonal expense – something to ramp up in an election year, outsource to consultants and scale back before Thanksgiving.

But persuasion is a year-round endeavor. Americans increasingly form impressions of politicians and institutions in digital spaces long before anyone shows them a campaign advertisement. Republicans figured this out years ago . The conservative media ecosystem runs whether or not President Trump is on the ballot. Its personalities build audiences and credibility daily, allowing Republican candidates to enter an election year as beneficiaries of work their campaigns never had to fund.

Democrats spent much of 2025 lamenting our inability to compete in that environment. Having finally shown some aptitude for it, we are watching some of the people responsible update their résumés.

What made the DNC’s operation work was distribution, not just production. And distribution depends on relationships that individual staffers spend months or years cultivating. So does the institutional knowledge that allows a digital team to recognize why one piece of content lands and another dies, or spot an opening in a news cycle before it closes. None of that is easily recovered by reposting the same job listings in 18 months.

There’s a fiscal case here, too. Democrats spend enormous sums on television advertising to reach voters they have often made little effort to engage between elections. Maintaining an audience is considerably more sensible than repeatedly paying to reach one from scratch.

Martin campaigned for the chairmanship on a promise to break up the Democratic consultant-industrial complex. The Bulwark reported earlier this year that his continued spending on consultants had drawn criticism from party officials. If the committee has to make hard financial decisions, keeping in-house digital talent with a demonstrated record of success should rank as a bigger priority.

The DNC is not a campaign that just wrapped. It is the permanent institution charged with advancing the party’s interests between elections. Over the next two years, Democrats will have to communicate the findings of congressional investigations, prosecute legislative fights, and make their case to voters who aren’t paying attention yet to the 2028 race.

The committee should protect year-round funding for its core digital content, rapid response and creator partnership teams, expanding them in election years rather than repeatedly rebuilding them. Mangubat’s team spent the better part of two years restoring what the party had stripped for parts. Now the party risks doing it again.

Between now and 2028, Democrats will spend millions on consultants hired to explain how we might better reach Americans online. We could start by keeping the people who already figured it out.

Kaivan Shroff was a 2024 DNC presidential delegate and worked as a digital organizer on Hillary Clinton’s 2016 campaign. He is an attorney and senior advisor to the Institute for Education, a non-profit in Washington .

articles.title: Flanagan says she ‘appreciates’ Schumer, but Van Hollen leads ‘like an organizer’
articles.summary: Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) on Sunday said she appreciated Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s (D-N.Y.) leadership and work in the upper chamber, but praised Sen. Chris Van Hollen’s (D-Md.) bid for leadership, saying that he leads “like an organizer.” CNN’s “State of the Union” host Dana Bash asked Flanagan if voters will “punish” senators who…
articles.body:
Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) on Sunday said she appreciated Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s (D-N.Y.) leadership and work in the upper chamber, but praised Sen. Chris Van Hollen’s (D-Md.) bid for leadership, saying that he leads “like an organizer.”

CNN’s “State of the Union” host Dana Bash asked Flanagan if voters will “punish” senators who chose Schumer over Van Hollen in the upcoming vote .

“What this is about is incorporating new voices into the party,” she said. “I appreciate Chuck Schumer. I like Chuck Schumer and appreciate his years of leadership. I simply think it is time for change. In the 2026 election, what we heard from voters is that they were pushing back against the status quo.”

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

Flanagan said this meant Democrats taking on the Trump administration but it also meant passing legislation like single-payer healthcare and raising the minimum wage.

“I’ve watched Chris Van Hollen lead like an organizer,” she continued. “I’ve watched him lead with courage and heart, and I think that that is what this moment really calls for, and so I am proud to support him and I know that we will all be unified after this leadership debate and conversation.”

Flanagan is one of two incoming senators, the other being Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.), who back Van Hollen for senate majority leader. He told NBC News’s Kristen Welker on “Meet the Press” that the focus is not on rejecting Schumer, saying he likes him “personally,” but “about embracing what Sen. Van Hollen has to offer.”

“This is a guy who both understands how the Senate works,” El-Sayed continued. “He’s been in the Senate for a long time. But also he’s demonstrated the ability to take some bold risks … And I think we have a moment right now where we need to take bold steps. The people are suffering.”

Van Hollen told Welker that his support is “north of 15 and momentum is in our direction.” He added that the election results were about “economic populism,” where Americans “are sick and tired of an economic system rigged in favor of the very wealthy against working people and fueled by political corruption.”

President Trump, facing a Democratic-controlled Congress starting in January, said on Sunday that working with Schumer if elected leader will be “very hard,” calling him “one of the worst [Senate majority leaders] in history.”

Schumer, who turns 76 years old on Monday has been leading the Senate Democratic Caucus since 2017. Van Hollen is less than 10 years younger than the minority leader at 67 years old.

The Democratic caucus will hold its election for majority leader on Dec. 1. Schumer has the support of 15 senators, while five senators have backed Van Hollen, according to The Hill’s whip list . A candidate needs 28 votes to win.

articles.title: Bessent compares tech outages to vaccines
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday seemed to compare the recent wave of technology outages at major U.S. banks to the temporary side effects of vaccines, arguing that disruptions caused by cybersecurity updates are a small price to pay for stronger protections against cyberattacks. In an interview with CBS News’s “Face the Nation,” Bessent sought…
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday seemed to compare the recent wave of technology outages at major U.S. banks to the temporary side effects of vaccines, arguing that disruptions caused by cybersecurity updates are a small price to pay for stronger protections against cyberattacks.

In an interview with CBS News’s “Face the Nation,” Bessent sought to reassure Americans about the security of their money after technical problems at some of the nation’s largest banks, including JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, last week left thousands of customers struggling to access banking services.

Host Margaret Brennan asked whether Americans should be worried about the safety of their financial institutions following the outages, which led some customers to withdraw cash.

BestReviews is reader-supported and may earn an affiliate commission.

“I think the American people should think of it as a vaccine,” Bessent told Brennan. “Your arm may hurt, you may feel a little bad the next day, but it increases your long-term immunity and resiliency.”

The Treasury secretary said the outages were caused by glitches that occurred as banks updated their security systems, rather than a broader failure of the financial system.

“The banks have been at the forefront of cybersecurity for decades,” Bessent said. “They experience attacks every day, every week, every month, and they are by far the most resilient companies in the U.S. economy,” he said

JPMorgan Chase attributed its outage Monday to a software bug in its hardware systems, telling The Hill there was no evidence of a cyberattack. The bank said customers could still access their accounts and funds, though some services were taking longer than usual.

The banking disruptions followed a series of widespread technology failures across the country, including a nearly 24-hour outage affecting Microsoft Outlook and Teams and a nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop that disrupted thousands of flights.

President Trump downplayed the outages Tuesday while speaking to reporters in Manila, Philippines, ahead of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit.

“It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and have all the money, things like that happen,” Trump said.

Lawmakers left Capitol Hill and headed home for the Thanksgiving recess this weekend after a jam-packed week of moving bills and confirming appointments, as the 119th Congress comes to a close and Democrats take control of both chambers in the new year.

“Dana, in different contexts, you can use a different word,” he replied. “The president pulling off that summit, getting the three of them together, is just remarkable.”

Virginia Foxx (R-N.C.) conceded to Democrat Chuck Hubbard in North Carolina’s 5th Congressional District after weeks of a high-profile race. “While I am saddened that I did not emerge victorious in this election, I continue to have great faith in our nation, our state and the people of North Carolina,” Foxx said in a statement.

“The peaceful transition of elected office from one person to another is one of the true hallmarks of our system of government, and I am proud to be a citizen of a nation that prizes fair and free elections,” she added.

articles.title: Foxx concedes to Hubbard in North Carolina House race
articles.summary: Outgoing Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-N.C.) reportedly conceded her race against Rep.-elect Chuck Hubbard (D-N.C.) following a high-profile recount process that saw the longtime lawmaker trailing behind her opponent. The Hill’s nonpartisan election results partner Decision Desk HQ projected Hubbard as the winner, at more than 330 votes or 48.74 percent of the vote to Foxx’s…
articles.body:
Outgoing Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-N.C.) reportedly conceded her race against Rep.-elect Chuck Hubbard (D-N.C.) following a high-profile recount process that saw the longtime lawmaker trailing behind her opponent.

The Hill’s nonpartisan election results partner Decision Desk HQ projected Hubbard as the winner, at more than 330 votes or 48.74 percent of the vote to Foxx’s 48.62 percent in the latest reported results.

“I recently called to congratulate Chuck Hubbard on his victory in this election, and I sent him my best wishes as he represents this wonderful district in the 120th Congress,” Foxx wrote in a statement shared with The Hill. “While I am saddened that I did not emerge victorious in this election, I continue to have great faith in our nation, our state and the people of North Carolina.”

“After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I’m humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short,” she continued.

Hubbard similarly confirmed on social media on Sunday Foxx had conceded the race “following the results of the recount process.”

Initial results showed Foxx trailing Hubbard by a small margin in the race to represent North Carolina’s 5th Congressional District. She previously requested a recount, citing state law allowing that candidates request one when the margin of victory is under 1 percent.

The Democrat ran on lowering the cost of living, supporting public education, expanding access to affordable health care and advocating against Medicare, Medicaid and Social Security cuts, according to his campaign website .

Hubbard was one of many North Carolina Democrats who ousted long-term incumbent Republican lawmakers. The Democratic wins in the Tar Heel State are consistent with the overall midterm results across the country, where the Democrats have taken control of the Senate and the House in a sweeping victory .

articles.body:
Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) said Sunday he is “optimistic” that Congress can pass a bipartisan artificial intelligence (AI) bill before the end of the year, despite a narrowing window for Republicans to advance legislation before Democrats take control of the House in January.

Obernolte, who chairs the House Republican Policy Committee, said lawmakers have made significant progress on the Great American AI Act (GAIA), a package of proposals establishing federal safeguards for the rapidly developing technology.

“I’m optimistic about our chances of getting something done in the current Congress,” Obernolte said in an interview with NewsNation’s “The Hill Sunday.”

“We have had major pieces of [GAIA] passed through the relevant policy committees, and they’re queued up for action on the House floor,” he told host Chris Stirewalt. “So we actually could get this done this year.”

The California Republican has been among the leading voices in Congress pushing for federal AI legislations as states move ahead with their own regulations, which has caused concerns in the industry over a patchwork of conflicting rules for tech companies operating nationwide.

“All the 50 states are going in 50 different directions on AI regulation,” he said, adding that lawmakers must strike a balance between protecting Americans from the misuse of AI and allowing the technology’s benefits to reach the economy.

The push comes as Democrats prepare to assume control of the House following this month’s midterm elections, potentially complicating efforts to reach an agreement on AI oversight.

Obernolte acknowledged that any legislation would require cooperation across party lines, regardless of which party controls Congress.

“At the end of the day, anything that we pass, regardless of who controls the House and who controls the Senate, whatever gets passed needs 60 votes in the Senate to avoid the filibuster, and it’s going to need the signature of the president of the United States,” he said.

He noted that GAIA has six bipartisan co-sponsors and that portions of the legislation have already attracted support from lawmakers in both parties.

“I’m optimistic that we can get the job done,” he said.

articles.body:
Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) on Sunday said the victories won by her and Sen.-elect Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) as the first Native American women to be in the U.S. Senate “makes our capitol look a little bit more like America.”

Flanagan told CNN’s Dana Bash on “State of the Union” that she didn’t run to “make history” after Bash pointed to a photo Flanagan posted of herself outside the Minnesota state House wearing a ribbon skirt, a traditional Indigenous dress for girls and women.

“But it is about time that a Native American woman served in the U.S. Senate, and I think it’s important for our democracy that it accurately reflects the people it seeks to represent,” Flanagan said.

“Having an Alaska Native woman and a Native American woman serving in the Senate –– that makes our capitol look a little bit more like America, and I think it helps us get better results,” the Minnesota Democrat said. “And I am excited to serve with her.”

Peltola’s win last week was the final Democratic victory in a sweeping turnout for the party in the 2026 midterm election. She defeated Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), becoming the 56th member of the Democratic majority in the Senate to be ushered in in January.

Flanagan is of Ojibwe and Irish descent, and a citizen of the federally-recognized White Earth Nation. Peltola is of Yu’pik and German American descent.

Both have served within their communities, with Flanagan helped form the Minnesota House Native American Caucus in the Minnesota state legislature and Peltola having been a member of the Orutsararmiut Traditional Native Council.

Several Indigenous candidates won victories on Election Day, from the federal level to the local level. Crystalyne Curley, Speaker of the Navajo Nation Council, won to become the first woman to be Navajo Nation president, leading the largest reservation in the country.

The House saw Reps. Sharice Davids (D-Kan.), Tom Cole (R-Okla.) and Josh Brecheen (R-Okla.) all reelected, with Davids from the Ho-Chunk Nation, Cole from the Chickasaw Nation and Brecheen from the Choctaw Nation.

Reps-elect Clair Valdez (D-N.Y.) of the Ysleta del Sur Pueblo and Sean McCann (D-Minn.) of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation were also both elected to Congress.

Former Interior Secretary Deb Haaland was elected to be New Mexico’s first Native American governor. She previously served under former President Biden as the the first Native American to serve as a secretary in a presidential Cabinet and the second to serve in the Cabinet. She and Davids were both the first Native American women to be elected to the House in 2018.

Former Vice President Charles Curtis of the Kaw Nation was the first Indigenous member of both the House and the Senate, according to the Senate’s website . He later served under former President Herbert Hoover from 1929 to 1933, and remains the only known Native American to hold such a high office.
